newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MANDELA'S KNEE FORCES ANOTHER DIARY CHANGE.
newsitem.headline: MANDELA'S KNEE FORCES ANOTHER DIARY CHANGE.

text.p: No one doubts that President Nelson Mandela's last-minute postponement of a four-nation trip to South East Asia was because of a sore knee, but diplomats said he was the only person who could get away with it.
Mandela, 78, phoned leaders in the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei at the weekend to say he was cancelling a visit due to start next Saturday.

"He can get away with it because people will forgive him virtually anything, but I cannot think of another world leader who could make so many last-minute changes and not lose credibility," a diplomat told Reuters.
Mandela has cancelled, postponed or cut short several foreign visits since he became the country's first democratically-elected president in April 1994.
Reasons given have included his health, which was undermined by 27 years in apartheid jails, exhaustion, and changed political circumstances in host countries.
He has postponed a visit to Israel twice already and has put a rescheduled November visit on hold following the renewed conflict in the region.
He cancelled a visit to Tanzania in August 1994, cut short a visit to India in January of the following year and has twice put off scheduled visits to Angola and to Russia.
Last year, Mandela triggered a storm when he told the Organisation of African Unity barely 48 hours before he was scheduled to speak that he would send Deputy President Thabo Mbeki in his place.
The South African department of foreign affairs gave no reason on Monday for the sudden announcement Mandela would not leave for Southeast Asia as planned.
President Fidel Ramos of the Philippines answered the riddle when he said in Manila that Mandela had phoned him personally, citing health reasons for cancelling the visit.
"That's what we are hearing, too," said a Western diplomat in Pretoria.
"Apparently the President's knee has not healed as quickly as his doctors had hoped and he would not be able to cope with the standing and walking of a four-nation trip," he said.
A spokeswoman for Mandela said he was still recovering from a September 14 operation to drain fluid from his right knee.
"The president is fine, but you probably saw when Queen Beatrix was here last week that his knee was causing him some discomfort," she said.
Another Western diplomat told Reuters there was little doubt that it was just Mandela's sore knee that caused him to cancel the trip at less than a week's notice.
"Mandela leads a charmed life. At the working level, people are probably pretty pissed off, but there is only one Mandela and everyone wants a piece of him on whatever terms," he said.
A third diplomat agreed that Mandela was possibly the only world leader who could cancel a state visit at short notice and be invited again the next week.
The South African rand currency crashed in February on a spate of rumours including one that Mandela was seriously ill.

In a bid to stem speculation about his health, he checked into a private hospital for a battery of tests that showed nothing more than ailments common to a man of his age and damage to his eyes caused by hard labour in a lime quarry.
